newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - S.Electric eyes balance sheet.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - S.Electric eyes balance sheet.

text.p: British regional electricity company (Rec), Southern Electric Plc, is committed to using its balance sheet strength to maximise shareholder value but has no immediate plans, finance director Ian Marchant told Reuters in an interview.

"We're committed to using the balance sheet strength to maximise shareholder value. We've got no immediate plans to do anything...we are awaiting to see how things evolve over the next few weeks," he said.
Southern, along with other privatised utilities, could be subject to a one-off tax proposed by the new Labour government on excess profits, details of which are expected in a first budget on July 2.
Marchant said Southern's gearing at the end of March was 25 percent and that the company recognised "the balance sheet is still not efficient".
Southern, which was outbid by Scottish Power last year in a battle to take over Southern Water, later announced a share buyback deal worth up to 156 million stg.

Marchant said he did not feel the company was now under pressure to make an acquisition, adding Southern was "confident" its existing businesses would allow dividend growth of five to eight percent in real terms over the next three years.
"There's more to go for in reducing costs in the distribution business," Marchant added, but declined to give targets.
Southern turned in annual pre-tax profits of 255.5 million pounds, within expectations, on Wednesday and paid out a dividend of 21.5 pence per share.

It said it intended to invest some 100 million pounds building seven gas-fired power stations with a total capacity of 300 megaWatts. Marchant said the first two should be on line in a year and should give "quite significant earnings growth from 2000 and beyond".
Southern's maximum demand last year was 5,700 mW, Marchant said.

Marchant said the company was "still talking quite seriously to two or three people" about link-ups for liberalisation of the electricity market in 1998, "and if there is a commercial deal to be done, we'll do it."
Southern would be ready to enter testing of the market in January and was "entirely confident" of being ready on time for the opening up of the market, scheduled for April 1998, Marchant said.
Last week, industry regulator Offer said it would consider penalties for any companies which fell behind schedule.
"The chance of us facing penalties is very remote," Marchant said.
"We see (liberalisation) as a source of earnings growth," he added, "we believe we can create shareholder value in that business."
